title: Trials, Wisdom, and Doing the Word

verses.text: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion: Greetings.
Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds,
because you know that the testing of your faith develops perseverance.
Allow perseverance to finish its work, so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything.
Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.
But he must ask in faith, without doubting, because he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.
That man should not expect to receive anything from the Lord.
He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
The brother in humble circumstances should exult in his high position.
But the one who is rich should exult in his low position, because he will pass away like a flower of the field.
For the sun rises with scorching heat and withers the plant; its flower falls and its beauty is lost. So too, the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
Blessed is the man who perseveres under trial, because when he has stood the test, he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him.
When tempted, no one should say, "God is tempting me." For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone.
But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed.
Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.
Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers.
Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow.
He chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creation.
My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger,
for man's anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.
Therefore, get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil, and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls.
Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves.
For anyone who hears the word but does not carry it out is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror,
and after observing himself goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like.
But the one who looks intently into the perfect law of freedom, and continues to do so—not being a forgetful hearer, but an effective doer—he will be blessed in what he does.
If anyone considers himself religious and yet does not bridle his tongue, he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless.
Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.

context.author: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (1:1). Tradition identifies him with James the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem.
context.genre: Letter with the feel of wisdom literature and a sermon
context.audience: Probably Jewish Christians living outside the land of Israel (“the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” 1:1). Some take the phrase as a title for all of God's people.
context.setting: James writes to scattered Jewish Christians, many of them under pressure. He opens with a surprising call to count trials as joy, because testing produces steadfastness. He then urges them to ask God for wisdom, to see that poverty and riches are temporary, and to be doers of the word and not hearers only.
context.custom: Polished metal mirrors (vv.23-24) gave a recognizable reflection, which is James's picture of a man who looks and then forgets what he saw. The Greek word for “religion” in v.27, threskeia, usually meant outward worship and ritual practice. James says that the worship that is pure before God includes caring for orphans and widows, whom the Law told Israel to protect (Deuteronomy 10:18).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 2 gives concrete tests of faith: favoritism and works.
context.timelineBible: James and Jesus run close at several points: asking God for good things (1:5; Matthew 7:7-11) and doing the words and not only hearing them (1:22; Matthew 7:24-27). The “perfect law of freedom” (1:25) is James's own phrase and he does not say which law; in 2:8 he calls the command to love your neighbor (Leviticus 19:18) the royal law. The “firstfruits” (v.18) recall the first of the harvest that Israel gave to God (Leviticus 23:10).
context.sparkNotes: Count it all joy when you meet trials, because the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. If any of you lacks wisdom, ask God, who gives generously. A double-minded man is unstable. Blessed is the one who endures trial. God tempts no one, but each is tempted by his own desire. Every good gift is from above. Be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. Be doers of the word and not hearers only. Pure religion is to visit orphans and widows and keep oneself unstained from the world.

translation.meaning: Literally “two-souled.” A word James may have coined.

otBackground.note: Wisdom is sought like silver, and the Lord gives it (compare James 1:5).
Job is tested and endures. James mentions him in 5:11.
Love your neighbor as yourself, the command James calls the royal law (2:8).

overview.summary: Trials produce endurance, God gives wisdom to those who ask, and real religion means doing the word by caring for the vulnerable.
overview.settingLine: From Jerusalem to the scattered tribes.

history.t: Paul calls James the Lord's brother and names him with Cephas and John as one who seemed to be a pillar of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19; 2:9). Josephus (Antiquities 20.200) says that a high priest named Ananus had James stoned, about AD 62.

Jewish communities lay across the Mediterranean world and beyond the Euphrates (Acts 2:9-11; Philo, Embassy to Gaius 281-283). James writes to "the twelve tribes of the Dispersion." Many take this to mean Jewish believers living outside the land of Israel, and some take it as a title for all of God's people.

customs.t: Mirrors were usually made of polished metal such as bronze. They gave a recognizable reflection, but a less clear one than modern glass. James uses one for a man who looks at his face and then forgets what he looked like (1:23-24).

With no father or husband to provide for them, orphans and widows were among the most exposed people of the ancient world. The Law told Israel to defend them (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 10:18), and James makes caring for them part of religion that is pure before God.

archaeology.t: Papyrus 23 is a leaf from a codex found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and dated to the 3rd century. It has James 1:10-12 on one side and 1:15-18 on the other. It shows that James was being copied in Egypt by the 200s.

A limestone bone box with an Aramaic inscription naming James, Joseph and Jesus was announced in 2002. Its owner said he bought it from a dealer, so it has no known findspot. An Israeli committee judged the inscription a modern forgery in 2003, while other experts disagreed. In 2012 a court acquitted the owner of forgery, but the judge said this did not prove the inscription genuine.

overview.discussion: James says to ask God for wisdom “without doubting.” What decision am I facing where I need to ask for wisdom?

historicalImage.caption: One side of Papyrus 23, a leaf from a codex of the letter of James found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and dated to the 3rd century (now in the Spurlock Museum, University of Illinois). This side has James 1:15-18: desire gives birth to sin, and every good gift comes down from above. It shows that James was copied and read in Egypt by the 200s.

currentImage.caption: The entrance of the Cathedral of St James in the Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem. The church honors two apostles named James, the son of Zebedee and James the brother of the Lord. The building is mostly from the 12th century, so it is a memorial of the tradition and not evidence from the first century. James the brother of Jesus led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9).
